1:
The delay of the kings puzzles them. Henry finds it strange twice over: strange they had not moved sooner, since Israel's design was no secret and no attempt was made to hold the crossing or relieve Jericho, and stranger that they moved now, when Jericho had proved God's power and Ai Israel's policy and the sensible end of a consultation was peace rather than war. He puts it down to presumption or despair, adding that many do not know the things belonging to their peace until they are hidden from their eyes. Calvin says the same as a judgment: their minds were intoxicated from above with security, and it was excessive stupor not to stand on guard until roused by the sack of two towns. He reads a mercy in it too, that God was sparing the weakness of his own people, whom the combined forces of so many nations would have alarmed, the interval letting them compose themselves. Wesley turns it the other way, wishing that Israel would learn from Canaanites who were often at variance among themselves and yet laid private interests aside against a common enemy.

Gibeon alone took the other road, and the commentators mark the divergence. Keil sets out the sequence: before the league was formed, the largest town of central Canaan, with the smaller towns dependent on it, anticipated the danger by a stratagem and succeeded, because Joshua and the elders fell into the snare without inquiring of the Lord; he quotes the judgment that the account warns the Church of every age against the cunning of a world seeking peaceable recognition from the kingdom of God. Henry makes the contrast the point: others heard the same news and were irritated into war, these heard it and were drawn into peace, as the gospel is to some a savour of life and to others of death, the same sun softening wax and hardening clay.

On Gibeon's standing they differ. Keil calls it one of the royal cities, larger than Ai and held by brave Hivites, later allotted to Benjamin and made a Levitical town, and the seat of the tabernacle from the destruction of Nob until Solomon's temple; he places it forty or fifty stadia from Jerusalem on the ancient estimate and identifies it with a village two hours to the north-west. Clarke takes it for the Hivite capital and follows the same later history. Gill and Henry notice what is absent: no king of Gibeon is ever mentioned, and both infer a government of elders, Henry adding that a single ruler's heart would have been too high to yield. Gill reports against himself an Arabic writer who has a king of Gibeon write to Joshua with large gifts and be restored to his throne. Ellicott adds that the town was one of a group of four.

On the ruse the verdicts divide between prudence and fraud. Ellicott sees a curious compensation in it: at Shechem long before, a single Hivite city was put to the sword by Israel through a stratagem, and here a stratagem saves four Hivite cities from that sword. Calvin grants that they judged rightly in resolving to bear anything rather than provoke God further by vain resistance, and notes how odious the attempt was to their neighbours, since it made a schism among them and opened a door to Israel. But he will not excuse the means. Fraud used towards the very people whose favour was wanted is absurd and at variance with equity, and he asks what stability a league so founded could have. The blame he lays on both sides, Joshua and the rulers being under no obligation to bargain rashly about a matter they had not investigated; and he states the principle that governs what follows, that Joshua bargained with mere masks and contracted no obligation except according to the words they had used.
4:
Whether the trick was easy to see through is the live question. Clarke says twice that it should have been, finding it strange that the Israelites suspected what they did and stranger that they then took so little care. Ellicott answers it. Israel had themselves come from a far country and their raiment had not waxed old on them these forty years, nor had their feet swelled; with manna they needed no bread; of worn garments and stale provisions they had no experience at all, so it is not unnatural that their eyes failed to detect the disguise. On the morality Clarke is brisk. Finesse of this kind is allowed by the practice of all nations and stratagems in war are held legal; but as to whether the Gibeonites lied, certainly they did, and the word of God neither commends them nor holds them up as examples. Plain submission would have served them better, since lying always defeats its own purpose while truth and honesty never wear out. Gill notices the emphatic word the version drops, that these also dealt craftily, and offers three comparisons: with the other nations, with Israel at Ai, and, from a rabbinic source, with Simeon and Levi at Shechem, whose victims were Hivites too.

The details attract the lexicographers. Ellicott reports that the verb rendered as making themselves ambassadors occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, and that a one-letter change turns it, in the Greek and Aramaic versions, into taking provision. Clarke works over the bread, spotted with age or pierced with holes by vermin, and over the English word for the mended shoes, tracing it to an old term for seamed or patched from a rag, though others derive it from a word for a nail. Gill says only that the worn shoes had been pieced with bits of leather. Clarke draws an inference from the request for a league, the verb being to cut a covenant sacrifice: heathenism then had its own sacrifices, covenants being ratified by offering to the gods and invoking them.

Calvin turns to the law. In strict law the covenant was null. What was stipulated when the petition was granted, except safety on the footing of coming from a remote region? Every repetition of the falsehood annuls further a compact drawn out by fraud, its real meaning amounting only to a promise not to molest a foreign people living far off; and the Israelites had expressly excluded the inhabitants of the land. Nothing could be gained by the fraud. Nor were they helped by the fallacious use of the divine name, pretending to have come because of the God of Israel and throwing a mist over Joshua's mind. Ellicott hears another assumption in the Israelites' question, that in asking whether these men dwelt among them they treated Canaan as already their own.

The interview is read as a study in artful reply. Clarke observes that they answered the elders' question only by calling themselves servants, and addressed that to Joshua rather than to them, having seen who was commander-in-chief; to his direct questions they gave an explicit answer made of truth, falsehood and hypocrisy mixed. Wesley finds the general submission itself suspicious, giving Joshua reason to think them Canaanites, and Gill adds an old observation that they offered to serve Joshua alone rather than the whole people, wanting him for their head. Two notice the same omission. Keil remarks that they say nothing of the crossing of the Jordan or the fall of Jericho, quoting the reason that men from a very distant region could not have heard by report of things so lately done; Wesley says the same. Clarke concedes that this portion of their account was strictly true, the fame of Egypt and of the two kings having reached the whole land, and Gill notes their care to magnify the distance while naming no country.
10:
What the princes did with the provisions is read four ways. Gill takes them to have handled the bread rather than eaten it, men in a plentiful country being unlikely to eat such stuff, and cites rabbinic authorities for whom its dryness was the convincing evidence. Clarke supposes a meal taken in friendship, eating together being there a token of unalterable friendship, so that men who have shared even salt reckon themselves in perpetual covenant. Gill knows that reading and argues against it, since a covenant meal would have been better provided. Ellicott changes the subject of the sentence, following the margin and the Aramaic: they accepted the men on the strength of their provisions, the men meaning the envoys. Clarke, who prefers the meal, still says it should not be hastily rejected. Calvin dismisses both tasting and covenant feast as insipid fictions, holding the clause to be an indirect censure of a credulity that fastened on the bread without noticing how little colour the story had.

On the failure to inquire of the Lord they are unanimous and severe. Keil names the neglected means, the Urim and Thummim of the high priest, and the substitute accepted, as though dry mouldy bread were a safe guarantee of truth. Clarke calls it highly reprehensible, this being a state transaction in which the interest and honour of God as their king were concerned. Henry turns it into a proverb, that we make more haste than good speed when we do not stay to take God with us, and adds that the fraud was soon found out, a lying tongue being but for a moment. Wesley draws the rule that in every business of importance we should consult God by word and prayer, since many an affair miscarries for want of it; he concedes that God would probably have consented to sparing the Gibeonites, but with more caution and an obligation to embrace the true religion. Calvin supplies the fact that makes the credulity indefensible: the Gibeonite capital stood some fourteen miles from Jericho and half that from Ai.

Henry describes the treaty as quickly and informally made. They agreed to let the Gibeonites live, and no more was asked; in an ordinary war a small thing, but in the wars of Canaan a great favour. He notes that Joshua did not act alone but with the princes, whom, for all his extraordinary call to the government, he treated as sharers in it rather than keeping them under foot. Keil observes that letting them live is the only article recorded, being the main point and because Canaanites ought properly to have been destroyed. Clarke, finding the same words as in the request, infers an ordinary covenant, a sacrifice offered and its blood poured out before the Lord.

Whether the league bound is argued from three directions. Keil denies that any express command was broken, since the law forbade treaties with Canaanites, which these were not supposed to be, the rule permitting terms applying to wars with foreign nations. Wesley gives three reasons for holding it lawful and obliging: that Joshua and all the princes on review concluded it so; that God punished its violation long afterwards; and that God is said to have hardened the other cities against seeking peace so that he might destroy them, which seems to imply that their destruction followed their own obstinacy rather than a peremptory command. Henry states principle and limit together: an oath unlawful in itself would not have bound, since no obligation can make it a duty to sin, but sparing Canaanites who submitted and left their idolatry was not unlawful, and a citizen of Zion swears to his own hurt and changes not. He adds what the princes did not do: seek release from the high priest, still less plead that no faith need be kept.
16:
The speed of the discovery is itself made an argument. Calvin treats it as a chastisement of their levity, the swiftness sharpening the shame, since sloth had made them stumble over a matter almost set before their eyes; and he sees a paternal indulgence in what followed, God turning to their good what might justly have hurt them, so that they marched quietly through that region and found free sustenance. Clarke supplies the measurement that supports the charge, Gibeon lying only some eight leagues from the camp, so three days were ample to expose the fraud. Gill says the treaty was concluded the very day the envoys arrived, they in haste lest they be found out and the Israelites taking no pains to inquire. Keil records the march that followed and the arrival at the four towns on the third day.

The towns then draw a good deal of later history. Ellicott divides them between two tribes, three to Benjamin and one to Judah, and finds there the explanation of a later episode, since the greater part of the Gibeonite territory lay in Benjamin and a king of that tribe was tempted to confiscate it for his followers, which he appears to have done at one town but not at all. Ellicott adds that Gibeon became a city of the priests and in time a principal place of worship and the seat of the tabernacle, as another of the four was of the ark. Clarke notices the same about the ark and draws a conclusion, that there is no evidence the preservation of the Gibeonites displeased the Lord.

The murmuring is explained by motive rather than principle. Clarke says they complained merely because they were deprived of the spoils, having come under the full influence of a predatory spirit, and adds that God, seeing the proneness, at times interdicted the spoils of conquered cities altogether. Wesley gives two causes, the desire of spoil and the general proneness of a people to censure its rulers. Gill records that the deception was established and they still did not strike; Keil gives the princes' reason, that they might not touch them because of their oath, lest wrath come upon them.

Why an oath got by fraud should hold is the question the passage forces. Clarke concedes the difficulty before answering it: the covenant rested on a supposition afterwards shown to be baseless, and the engagement was therefore vitiated and void on the part of the deceived; yet because the elders had eaten with them, offered a covenant sacrifice and sworn by the divine name, they held themselves not at liberty to break its terms as far as life was concerned. He argues that this pleased God from a silence and a judgment: Joshua is nowhere reprehended, and a king who four centuries later thought himself loosed and destroyed the Gibeonites was punished. Ellicott is briefer and sharper: obtained by false pretences or not, the covenant was made in the name of the Lord and so was his, and could not be broken; and the law, he adds, had raised the tone of morality in just this particular, since many Christians would not hesitate to repudiate an agreement concluded under false pretences. Calvin, who had called the compact null in strict law, now poses two questions formally, whether men who never meant to pledge faith to impostors contracted any obligation, and whether the people might rescind what their leaders had foolishly promised; and he answers from the general position that the obligation of an oath is to be held in the greatest sacredness, so that we may not resile on the plea of error even from pacts in which we were deceived, the name of God being more precious than the wealth of a whole world. The editor of the block marks the appearance of inconsistency between that and his earlier verdict.
20:
Calvin reads the settlement as a compromise and says so plainly. The lives are given according to agreement, but the covenant is ratified only in part, since men entitled to be made perfectly secure are stripped of liberty, which is dearer than life. From this he infers that Joshua and the rest, in doubt and perplexity, devised a middle course so as not to make the oath altogether void; the chief object was to appease the multitude, while the fraud was still punished, so that impunity should not increase the derision. He does not soften the terms: it was a harsh condition, not merely servile labour but removal from their homes to a wandering life, and the office was as mean as it was laborious. Gill hears the same doubleness in the princes' phrase, which may name either the sparing of their lives or the punishment not yet spoken; and he notes how importunate they were about the lives, because of the oath.

What the service amounted to is described more narrowly by some than by others. Clarke suspects a proverbial expression for the lowest state of servitude, while allowing that it may be meant literally. Wesley takes it literally and divides it, one kind of drudgery standing for the rest: they were public servants, partly for the sacrifices and services of God's house, which Israel would otherwise have performed, partly for the camp, and sometimes for particular Israelites. Keil is stricter, reading the sentence as a curse of perpetual servitude, the idiom meaning that a servant shall never be cut off from among them, and taking the definition to be labour for the house of God, which the law assigns to the lowest classes of the people. He connects the whole arrangement with the ancient curse pronounced upon Canaan.

The summons itself is read as a change of parties. Henry supposes that by now it was not the original messengers who were treated with but the elders of Gibeon and its dependent cities, so that the matter might be fully compromised, and Wesley thinks the same; Gill has the envoys detained at Gilgal until the party returned, and brought before Joshua on their report. What Henry chiefly notices is the manner of the reproof. Joshua gives it very mildly, loading them with no ill names and no provoking language, not calling them, as they deserved, base liars, but only asking why they had beguiled him; and Henry draws the lesson that under the greatest provocation it is our wisdom and duty to keep our temper and bridle our passion, since a just cause needs no anger to defend it and a bad one is never the better for it.

On what makes the sentence just the two who argue it agree. Calvin observes that Joshua, having a severe sentence to deliver, first shows that no injustice is involved, since nothing would be more unbecoming than to let wiles profit the men who use them; he expostulates before he pronounces, and by that order throws the blame of the servitude back on men who bear nothing worse than their own guile deserved. Calvin admits the hardest feature, that no term is set to the labour, the words meaning that slaves shall never cease from among them, and answers that they were cursed of their own accord. Henry reports the best excuse the case would bear, that they had found a sentence of death passed on them in the word of God and no opposing it in his works; considering that his sovereignty is incontestable, his justice inflexible and his power irresistible, they resolved to try what his mercy was, and found it not in vain to cast themselves upon it.
23:
The sentence is referred back to Noah by all who touch it. Gill takes them to be shown as the posterity of cursed Canaan, not exempted by their artifice, and finds the old words fulfilled in their serving the Levites, who were themselves servants to the priests, and the seed of Shem from whom Israel sprang; he suggests they were spared so that this part of the curse might stand. Clarke answers the same question more strictly, that the curse of Ham implied slavery and nothing else, and that nothing but perpetual slavery is implied here: they were put under tribute, did the meanest offices, had their national importance annihilated, and were never allowed to incorporate with Israel, matching a servile caste he had met with elsewhere. Wesley makes it a change in the quality of the curse rather than an escape from it, the bondage being proper to their race by that ancient decree and entailed on their posterity.

Gill alone turns the sentence round. Mean as the office was, it gave them a place in the sanctuary and the chance of learning God's law and true worship, so that the curse became a blessing and they stand as an emblem and pledge of the reception of the Gentiles into the church. Two others draw a wider historical conclusion. Clarke supposes this to have been God's purpose towards all the Canaanite nations, that those who would not renounce their idolatry were to be extirpated and those who did preserved alive as tributaries and slaves. Ellicott reaches nearly the same place from the later history, the precedent seeming to have been followed by Solomon with the undestroyed remnant of the doomed nations; and he draws the inference plainly, that so large a body of surviving Canaanites should be remembered when the edict about the seven nations is considered, the sentence clearly not having been executed on the mass of the non-resisting population.

Whether these are the Nethinim of the later books is disputed. Wesley says they are, the durable part of their servitude being in the tabernacle and then the temple, whence the name, their service to the congregation at large ceasing once Israel was settled. Gill reports the same derivation, from the verb by which Joshua gave them to the sanctuary. Ellicott supports it from the returned captives, where the Nethinim are enumerated after the Levites, singers and porters, and the children of Solomon's servants coupled with them. Clarke will not have it: they are not mentioned after the captivity, Saul's persecution having, he thinks, nearly annihilated them, and there is no decisive proof, the Nethinim being probably slaves of a different race.

The plea and the settlement close the chapter. Keil states the excuse simply, that having heard of the command given through Moses they feared greatly for their lives and readily submitted to the resolution laid before them. Clarke makes the motive a law of nature, self-preservation dictating their measures, and admires their surrender, which expects justice because they had deceived and mercy because fear drove them to it, an appeal full of delicacy and cogent argument. Wesley hears them referring themselves to Joshua's piety and faithfulness to his oath, and turns it into a prayer to submit likewise to Christ. On the outcome Clarke distributes the two exactly: in the deliverance from the people's hands, mercy, and in the labour imposed, justice, so that Joshua did nothing but what was right in the eyes of the Lord as well as his own. Keil ends on a point of dating: the clause about the place God would choose does not mean they were sent there at once but that they were sentenced to serve at the altar wherever the sanctuary should stand; and while unto this day shows the account was written after the event, the future tense shows it was written before the choice.
